narrative:
The model predicts you have a 31% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to help you graduate.

The three factors that most strongly shaped this prediction were your reason for choosing the school, your lack of desire to pursue higher education, and your history of past failures. Your reason for choosing this school based on its reputation was the strongest influence overall, and it actually pushed the model toward thinking you would pass. However, this positive effect was outweighed by the other two factors.

The fact that you do not want to continue to higher education was the second most important driver and strongly pushed the prediction toward failing. Among students who passed, every single one expressed a desire for higher education, making your response quite unusual and concerning to the model. Similarly, having three past class failures was the third most important factor and also pushed strongly toward a failing prediction. Students who passed had zero past failures on average, so your history stands out sharply as a risk signal.

To improve, you should seriously reflect on your goals after school and consider whether building clearer motivation for further study could change your trajectory. Reducing future absences, which are already more than double the average of students who passed, and seeking extra academic support could also make a real difference. Taking the remedial courses seriously is a good first step toward turning this around.
